notes.definition: Alkenes contain the C=C functional group. They burn in oxygen like other hydrocarbons but tend to give smoky flames, and they react with hydrogen, water and the halogens by addition: atoms add across the C=C double bond, which becomes a single C–C bond.
explanation: The reactions of alkenes are controlled by their functional group, the carbon to carbon double bond (C=C). Alkenes react with oxygen in combustion reactions in the same way as other hydrocarbons. In plenty of oxygen, complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water, for example C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O. However, alkenes tend to burn in air with smoky (sooty) yellow flames, because combustion is often incomplete: some carbon forms soot (carbon particles) and carbon monoxide instead of carbon dioxide.

Most other reactions of alkenes are addition reactions. In an addition reaction, atoms add across the C=C double bond, so the double bond becomes a single C–C bond and a single product is formed. The molecule goes from unsaturated to saturated. Alkenes react in this way with hydrogen, with water (as steam) and with the halogens chlorine, bromine and iodine.

With hydrogen, alkenes form alkanes. This reaction is called hydrogenation and needs a catalyst, such as nickel, and heating. For example, ethene + hydrogen → ethane: C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆. Hydrogenation is used to harden vegetable oils, which contain C=C bonds, to make margarine. With water, alkenes form alcohols. Steam and the alkene are passed over a catalyst (such as phosphoric acid) at a high temperature and pressure. For example, ethene + steam → ethanol: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH. This is how much industrial ethanol is made.

With halogens, alkenes react quickly at room temperature, with no catalyst needed. One halogen atom adds to each carbon atom of the double bond. For example, ethene + bromine → dibromoethane: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂. Chlorine gives dichloro compounds and iodine gives diiodo compounds. This addition of bromine is the reaction behind the bromine water test: orange bromine is used up, so the solution turns colourless.

You should be able to draw the displayed formula of the product of any of these reactions for the first four alkenes. Start by drawing the alkene, change the double bond to a single bond, then add one atom (or group) from the reacting molecule to each of the two carbon atoms that were in the double bond. With hydrogen add H and H, with a halogen add X and X, and with water add H to one carbon and OH to the other. Check each carbon has four bonds.
keyFacts: The functional group of alkenes is C=C.
Alkenes burn with smoky flames because of incomplete combustion.
Addition reaction: atoms add across the C=C, which becomes a single C–C bond.
Alkene + hydrogen → alkane (catalyst, e.g. nickel, and heat): hydrogenation.
Alkene + steam → alcohol (catalyst, high temperature and pressure): hydration.
Alkene + halogen → dihaloalkane, at room temperature: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂.
Ethene + bromine → dibromoethane; this is why bromine water decolourises.
Addition reactions turn an unsaturated alkene into a saturated product.

keyTerms.definition: A reaction in which atoms add across a C=C double bond to form a single product with a single C–C bond.
Addition of hydrogen to an alkene, using a catalyst, to form an alkane.
Addition of water (steam) to an alkene, using a catalyst, to form an alcohol.
Addition of a halogen such as bromine to an alkene to form a dihalo compound.
The group of atoms responsible for the characteristic reactions of a compound; C=C in alkenes.
Burning in a limited supply of oxygen, producing carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot) as well as water.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up, such as nickel in hydrogenation.

workedExamples.title: Product of propene and bromine
workedExamples.question: Write the formula and describe the displayed formula of the product when propene reacts with bromine.
steps: Propene is C₃H₆ with the double bond between C1 and C2.
Bromine adds across the double bond: one Br on C1 and one Br on C2.
The C=C becomes a single bond. Formula: C₃H₆ + Br₂ → C₃H₆Br₂.
workedExamples.answer: C₃H₆Br₂ (dibromopropane): a three-carbon chain with only single bonds, Br on each of the first two carbons, and 6 H atoms.

workedExamples.title: Balancing alkene combustion
workedExamples.question: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of propene, C₃H₆.
steps: Oxygen atoms on the right: 6 + 3 = 9, so 4½O₂.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think addition reactions produce two products, like displacement.
misconceptions.right: In fact an addition reaction gives a single product: all the atoms of both reactants end up in one molecule.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often keep the double bond in the product.
misconceptions.right: In fact the C=C double bond becomes a single C–C bond when atoms add across it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think alkenes burn with a clean blue flame like methane.
misconceptions.right: In fact alkenes tend to burn with smoky yellow flames because combustion is often incomplete.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often add both bromine atoms to the same carbon.
misconceptions.right: In fact one bromine atom adds to each of the two carbon atoms that were joined by the double bond.

realWorld: Hydrogenation with a nickel catalyst hardens vegetable oils to make margarine and spreads.
Ethanol for industrial solvents and fuel is made by hydrating ethene from cracking.
Bromine water is used in labs and quality control to check whether an oil or fat is unsaturated.
separateOnlyContent: All of this subtopic is for separate Chemistry (8462) only. Combined Science students need only the bromine water test for alkenes (in Cracking and alkenes).
examTips: Give conditions for each reaction: hydrogen needs a catalyst (e.g. nickel); steam needs a catalyst plus high temperature and pressure; halogens react at room temperature.
When drawing products, check: no double bond left, one new atom or group on each of the two carbons, four bonds on every carbon.
Name products clearly: alkane (from hydrogen), alcohol (from water), dibromo/dichloro compound (from halogens).
Explain smoky flames by incomplete combustion, producing soot (carbon).
summary: Alkenes burn but often with smoky flames (incomplete combustion).
Alkenes undergo addition reactions across the C=C bond.
Alkene + H₂ → alkane, with a catalyst.
Alkene + steam → alcohol, with a catalyst, high temperature and pressure.
Alkene + halogen → dihalo compound, at room temperature.
In every addition the C=C becomes a single C–C bond.

flashcards.back: Atoms add across the C=C double bond to form one product; the double bond becomes a single bond.

questions.question:
An alkene reacts with steam.
What type of compound is formed?
questions.explanation: H adds to one carbon and OH to the other, forming an alcohol such as ethanol.

questions.question: Why do alkenes often burn in air with a smoky flame?
options: They have very high boiling points
Combustion is often incomplete, producing soot
markScheme: 1 mark: incomplete combustion producing soot / carbon
questions.explanation: Alkenes tend to undergo incomplete combustion in air, producing carbon particles (soot) that make the flame smoky.

questions.question:
Hydrogen can be added to an alkene.
Which catalyst is used?
questions.explanation: Hydrogenation uses a nickel catalyst (with heat). Yeast is used in fermentation and iron in the Haber process.

questions.question:
Propene, C₃H₆, reacts with chlorine.
What is the formula of the product?
questions.explanation: Addition keeps all atoms: C₃H₆ + Cl₂ → C₃H₆Cl₂. No hydrogen is lost, so C₃H₅Cl is wrong.

questions.question:
An alkene takes part in an addition reaction.
What happens to the C=C double bond?
options: It breaks and the molecule splits into two
It becomes a single C–C bond
markScheme: 1 mark: becomes a single C–C bond
questions.explanation: One of the two bonds opens and the new atoms bond to the carbons; the carbon chain stays joined by a single bond.

questions.question:
Ethanol can be made from ethene.
Which conditions are used?
options: Steam, a catalyst, high temperature and high pressure
markScheme: 1 mark: steam, catalyst, high temperature and pressure
questions.explanation: Hydration needs steam passed over a catalyst (e.g. phosphoric acid) at high temperature and pressure. Yeast at 30 °C is fermentation of sugar, a different route to ethanol.

questions.question:
Butene, C₄H₈, reacts with hydrogen.
What is the formula of the product?
questions.explanation: C₄H₈ + H₂ → C₄H₁₀ (butane). Adding H₂ gives the alkane with 2n + 2 hydrogen atoms.

questions.question:
Ethene reacts with bromine.
C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂
Calculate the mass of bromine that reacts with 14 g of ethene.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12   H = 1   Br = 80
questions.explanation: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ is a 1 : 1 reaction. Mr of Br₂ = 160.

questions.question:
Ethene reacts with steam.
Write a word equation for this reaction.
questions.explanation: Hydration of ethene gives ethanol, the alcohol with two carbon atoms.

questions.question:
Ethene reacts with hydrogen.
Write a balanced symbol equation for this reaction.
Name the catalyst used.
questions.explanation: Hydrogen adds across the double bond to make ethane. A nickel catalyst is used with heat.

1 mark: each carbon bonded to one Cl atom and two H atoms
questions.explanation: The product is dichloroethane, C₂H₄Cl₂. The double bond has gone and each carbon has four single bonds.

questions.question:
A student shakes bromine water with an alkene.
Table 1 shows the results.
Explain why the bromine water turns colourless.
markScheme: 1 mark: bromine reacts with / adds across the C=C double bond (addition)
1 mark: the orange bromine is used up / the product is colourless
questions.explanation: The orange colour comes from bromine. When bromine adds to the alkene it is used up, forming a colourless dibromo compound.

questions.question:
Propene, C₃H₆, burns completely in oxygen.
Write a balanced symbol equation for this reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct products, 3CO₂ and 3H₂O per propene
questions.explanation: 9 oxygen atoms per propene molecule needs 4½O₂, so double everything.

questions.question:
Pentene, C₅H₁₀, reacts separately with hydrogen, with steam and with iodine.
Give the molecular formula of the product of each reaction.
questions.explanation: In each case add the atoms of the reacting molecule to C₅H₁₀: + H₂, + H₂O, + I₂.

questions.question:
An alkene reacts with hydrogen.
Explain why this reaction is described as an addition reaction.
Explain why the product is saturated.
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogen atoms add across the C=C to form a single product
1 mark: the product has only single C–C bonds (an alkane), so it is saturated
questions.explanation: Nothing is removed; the two reactants combine into one molecule, and the double bond becomes single.

questions.question:
Describe the reactions of ethene with hydrogen and with steam.
In your answer, include the products, the conditions and balanced equations.
markScheme: Indicative content: ethene + hydrogen → ethane, C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆; catalyst (nickel) and heat; ethene + steam → ethanol, C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH; catalyst (e.g. phosphoric acid), high temperature and high pressure; both are addition reactions across C=C.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both reactions with correct products, conditions and equations.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): products of one or both reactions with limited conditions or equations.
questions.explanation: Remember: hydrogen gives an alkane, water gives an alcohol, and both need a catalyst.

questions.question:
Butene, C₄H₈, is an alkene.
Describe and explain the reactions of butene with oxygen, hydrogen, water and bromine.
In your answer, include the products formed, the conditions and how the structure of butene changes.
markScheme: Indicative content: oxygen: combustion, complete gives CO₂ and H₂O, C₄H₈ + 6O₂ → 4CO₂ + 4H₂O; tends to burn with a smoky flame due to incomplete combustion (soot, CO); hydrogen: catalyst (nickel), heat, forms butane C₄H₁₀; water: steam, catalyst, high temperature and pressure, forms butanol C₄H₉OH; bromine: room temperature, forms dibromobutane C₄H₈Br₂, bromine water decolourised; hydrogen, water and bromine are addition reactions; atoms add across C=C, which becomes a single C–C bond; product is saturated; one atom or group adds to each carbon of the double bond.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all four reactions described with correct products and conditions, and a clear explanation of addition across the double bond.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least three reactions with mostly correct products and some conditions, with some reference to addition.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two reactions with basic products.
questions.explanation: Check the combustion equation: 4 C gives 4CO₂, 8 H gives 4H₂O, oxygen atoms 8 + 4 = 12, so 6O₂.

questions.question:
Ethene reacts with iodine.
Which statement about this reaction is correct?
options: The product is C₂H₃I and HI
The double bond remains in the product
questions.explanation: Iodine adds across the double bond to give one product, C₂H₄I₂ (diiodoethane). Halogens add without a catalyst.

questions.question: Give the functional group that is responsible for the addition reactions of alkenes.
questions.explanation: The double bond is where atoms add during addition reactions.

questions.question: Give the type of compound formed when an alkene reacts with hydrogen.
questions.explanation: Adding H₂ across the C=C gives a saturated hydrocarbon: an alkane.
